title: How Ultraprocessed Foods Work
summary: Josh and Chuck explain ultra processed foods (UPFs), starting with Carlos Monteiro's NOVA food classification system (2010) with its four groups, then covering how UPFs grew out of World War II military food research (drying, intermediate moisture foods, Logan bar, cheese powder), the role of cheap subsidized corn and high fructose corn syrup, the health evidence including the 2019 NIH Kevin Hall controlled trial, the food culture and time critique, government dietary guidance in the US versus Brazil, and the listener mail about kidney transplants.
topics: World War II military food research
impossible burger and plant based meat
food deserts and cost of whole foods

entities.name: National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases

segments.title: Opening and introduction to ultra processed foods
segments.summary: The hosts introduce ultra processed foods as junk food viewed through science and public health, note they are entrenched in culture, and mention that many everyday foods fall into the category based on long ingredient lists.

segments.title: Origin of the NOVA system and the four food groups
segments.summary: Brazilian epidemiologist Carlos Monteiro proposed the NOVA classification in 2010 after noticing obesity and type 2 diabetes rising while sugar purchases fell. The hosts explain the four groups, from unprocessed or minimally processed foods to ultra processed foods, and how to recognize them by ingredients and marketing.

segments.title: Sponsor break
segments.summary: Short mid-show break; the hosts transition to the history of UPFs.

segments.title: World War II military food research and early processed foods
segments.summary: Anastasia de Sousa's book Combat Ready Kitchen calls World War II the big bang of ultra processed foods. The hosts discuss military food R&D including drying food and coffee, intermediate moisture foods, the Logan bar, and the origins of the Power Bar, and the Army's role in cheese processing.
topics: World War II military food research

segments.title: Cheese powder and cheese dust
segments.summary: George Sanders, a USDA dairy scientist, developed methods to dry cheese at low temperature so proteins encapsulate fats, enabling sliced cheese and cheese powder. The hosts note confusion over who first invented cheese powder and discuss Cheetos-style cheese dust snacks.

segments.title: Corn, subsidies, and high fructose corn syrup
segments.summary: The hosts explain how US corn yields increased and government subsidies made corn cheap, so it became a base ingredient. A single corn kernel yields corn oil, fiber, starch, gluten, and high fructose corn syrup, with HFCS produced by processing dextrose further. They mention The Dorito Effect and industrial uses of corn starch.

segments.title: Food culture, time, and critiques of home cooking advice
segments.summary: The hosts discuss Monteiro and Pollan's emphasis on food culture and shared family meals, the time required to cook whole foods, and critiques that this advice ignores time constraints, income, and the historical unpaid labor of cooking. Pollan's rules of thumb such as eat food, not too much, mostly plants are mentioned.
topics: eat food not too much mostly plants

segments.title: Health evidence and the 2019 Kevin Hall NIH study
segments.summary: The hosts describe UPFs being engineered to be hyperpalatable and less satiating, and Monteiro's view that they are intrinsically unhealthy. They present the 2019 NIH randomized controlled trial led by Kevin Hall with twenty participants, in which the ultra processed diet, matched for calories, led to about five extra calories per day eaten and about two pounds gained over two weeks.

segments.title: Policy, government guidance, and reformulation
segments.summary: The hosts discuss environmental concerns about crop monoculture and packaging waste, Brazil's food guidelines based on NOVA, other countries following, the US lacking an official UPF position and the McGovern controversy, and ideas for reformulating foods. The episode closes with a note on plant-based meat and a listener mail segment about kidney transplants.
